prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement of time

statement.case_for: After reading the openings I move optical lattice clocks from second place to my preferred prize. It is the only candidate that eight of eight members ranked, and five placed in the top three, which is a sign that the committee agrees on the substance and not only on a taste for one subfield. The physics is a clean idea (the magic wavelength, which cancels the light shift of the trap) turned into an experimental capability at the 1e-18 level that is reproduced in many national and university laboratories, with agreeing intercomparisons. The result is not only a better instrument: it opens a regime in which gravitational redshift is resolved over millimetres, and in which many-body effects and searches for variation of constants become measurable. The two-name credit (Katori for the concept and first realization, Ye for taking it to record accuracy and for many-body clock physics) is compact and defensible. From my own field I know how rare it is for a proposal to be both this simple and this robust across laboratories.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty after the 2005 prize (frequency combs and laser-based precision spectroscopy) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control). A sceptical reader can call lattice clocks the best next step in an already honoured line, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest practical consequence is still ahead. There is also a credit question about other strontium and ytterbium groups and about the junior people who built the clocks, which I cannot settle from the packet.

responses.point: Kroll ranked lattice clocks first because progress is limited by how precisely we can measure, and he sees this as a clean two-person configuration, while noting the committee might treat it as an extension of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the merit argument and with the two names. On the overlap, I think the difference is substantive: a comb is a ruler for optical frequency and an ion clock uses a single trapped particle, whereas the lattice clock needed a new idea, the magic-wavelength trap, to interrogate many neutral atoms at once without shifting the transition. That is what led to the 1e-18 stability and the many-body clock physics. I do not accept that this is merely incremental, but I accept that it is the main point we must defend in the committee. I am less persuaded by Kroll's second choice, atom interferometry (B057), because the priority story is entangled with Chu and Borde, who are not on the list.

responses.point: Olsson noted that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits reduces the near-term appetite for another superconducting-circuit prize, and she ranked circuit QED only sixth.
responses.response: She is right, and this is why I have reordered my own preference away from circuit QED, which I ranked first in the opening. The 2025 award covered quantum behaviour of a circuit, and circuit QED is a different physical step (strong light-matter coupling on a chip), but to the wider community the distinction is thin and the subject is close to my own work and to the centre I direct. I think it is wiser to let some time pass. I also disagree in part with her first choice, aberration-corrected electron optics (B013): it is an overdue instrument, but I find the physics-discovery content weaker than for B015, and the omission of Krivanek from the credited names is a fairness problem.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a clear case of theory followed by decisive experiment, with a new field of moire quantum matter, though lattice clocks only fifth.
responses.response: I take the theory-to-experiment argument seriously, and I see the same virtue in the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction. My reservation is maturity and not merit. The single-particle flat band is well understood, but the origin of the superconductivity and the role of twist-angle disorder are unsettled, and I recall that colleagues in other fields also describe sample-to-sample variation as large. Lattice clocks are reproduced across laboratories with agreeing numbers, which is a stronger reproducibility criterion. I would not object to B006 in a later year, and I would support it if the committee judges the field has stabilised.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked lattice clocks first and argued that other groups (PTB, NIST, JILA, SYRTE, RIKEN) are strong confirmation, not missing co-laureates, and that the step is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree and will use that framing: independent confirmation is the evidence of robustness that we want, and it need not be read as a claim on the prize. Where I add a qualification is that her atom-physics knowledge of the strontium history is better than mine, so I would ask her to state whether the early lattice-clock proposals of others affect Katori's priority. I also see her second choice, topological insulators (B055), as my first fallback.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that lattice clocks are a distinct step after the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or will see them as incremental.
Timing relative to the pending redefinition of the second: recognition now could be called either timely or early.
Exact priority among early lattice-clock proposals and the weight of other strontium and ytterbium groups, which I am recalling from memory.
For B055, how to handle the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit and the overlap with the 2016 topological prize.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits, so I have a clear subject and institutional connection to B024 (circuit QED) and would recuse myself on that candidate, or at least declare it. My field also makes me close to Chalmers colleagues in related areas. I have no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, or the other candidates in my preferred configuration that is apparent from my profile.
